vignette:
Matiu, a 67-year-old widowed interior designer of Pacific Islander background, came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had quietly narrowed around one ordeal he still could not fully put into words. He had been taken captive while working overseas, held in a concrete room with no clear sense of time, and repeatedly jolted by shouting in Arabic from men outside the door. What stayed with him was not only the danger but the helplessness of being unable to predict what would happen next, trapped in a space so enclosed that even now he felt the walls of that room seemed to follow him. Since returning home, he found that a sudden memory of the event could arrive without warning—while he was laying out fabric samples, driving, or standing at the sink—and the memory often came with the same useless, immediate fear he had felt there. At those moments his body tensed before he could think, his chest tightening and his attention snapping to exits and corners, as if danger might break in at any second.

Matiu had come to believe that if he did not prepare himself perfectly, he would be caught off guard again. Before any interaction, even a brief exchange with a client or a neighbor, he rehearsed exactly what he would say, sometimes several times, because the sudden intrusion of the captivity memory left him afraid he would lose his composure, say something foolish, or be unable to protect himself. He also began avoiding enclosed spaces, choosing open corridors or doorways when he could, and on difficult days he skipped work altogether rather than enter small meeting rooms, storage closets, or lift into a confined elevator. The effort of keeping the event at a distance seemed to keep it active in him; the less he let himself speak about the captivity, the more forcefully the memory broke through, as if his mind had been holding it in place all along. In his interior design practice, where he once moved confidently through clients’ homes and showrooms, he now arranged site visits around his fear of cramped spaces and would turn down jobs that required extended time in compact apartments. The more he organized his words and his movements, the more he felt able to hold himself together, yet the rehearsing kept him alert to threat; he was constantly checking how he might be trapped, cornered, or embarrassed, and that vigilance left him exhausted and edgy.

What frightened Matiu most was how quickly strong negative emotions flooded him when the memory or the sound of Arabic shouting surfaced. A raised voice in a market, or a television dialogue he could not immediately place, could send him back into the panic and shame of captivity, and from there he became more certain that danger was near. Living at that pitch of threat, he found that ordinary details around him began to read like warnings — a corridor door left ajar, a sudden pause in conversation, even a parked car idling too long outside his building could catch his attention and feel loaded with danger. He insisted on sitting with his back against a wall where he could see the room, whether he was in a café or waiting for an appointment, because anything less made him feel exposed and vulnerable. His fear sharpened his attention to every sound and movement, and that state of constant alertness made the old memories more likely to break through; when he was on edge, fragments of the event seemed to return more vividly, including words and shouts he sometimes heard in his head as if they were happening again. At times he could describe what happened only in pieces, then lose the thread completely, his face blank as he said the memory felt numb and far away, as though it had happened to a stranger. Other times, just trying to explain it made the room disappear from him altogether, and he would stop mid-sentence, unable to continue. Those gaps left him frustrated and ashamed, and after each failed attempt to tell the story he felt even more unsettled, as if the experience remained unresolved and therefore still dangerous.

Over the weeks and months, Matiu’s careful routines brought only temporary relief. The more he avoided work spaces that felt enclosed and the more he rehearsed every conversation, the smaller and more effortful his world became. He missed projects, withdrew from colleagues, and began saying no to invitations that would have required him to sit in unfamiliar rooms. His widowhood made the narrowing more painful; at home he had no one who knew the whole story, and in the quiet evenings the sudden memories and the voices he seemed to hear in his head were harder to push away. By the time he sought help, he was tired of organizing his day around escape routes and of feeling that his own body betrayed him before his mind could catch up. He wanted to understand why a sound, a room, or a passing flash of memory could still seize him so completely, and he was most afraid that unless something changed he would keep retreating from work, from people, and from the life he had rebuilt after captivity.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows rehearsal and avoidance increasing alertness and exhaustion, but it does not clearly say these strategies cause the traumatic memory to return or intensify.
The vignette shows triggers like a raised voice or Arabic shouting provoking fear and memories, but it does not state that the sense of threat itself leads to new triggers or reminder cues.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette shows rehearsal and avoidance increasing alertness and exhaustion, but it does not clearly say these strategies cause the traumatic memory to return or intensify.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows triggers like a raised voice or Arabic shouting provoking fear and memories, but it does not state that the sense of threat itself leads to new triggers or reminder cues.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
